subject: design
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Concept of the skill, Coverage, Philosophy of the skill, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and standard perception/Gestalt-based hierarchy practice (scale/weight/contrast/color/position/isolation as stacking signals, suppression over amplification, the squint and grayscale tests).

cases.scenario: A dashboard renders 14 widgets at the same size, weight, and color. Every number is bold, every card has a heavy border, and users say they 'don't know where to look.'
cases.context: No content can be removed; all 14 metrics are required by the business.
cases.question: How should the agent re-establish hierarchy?
expected_flags: Suppress secondary widgets (lighter weight, lower contrast, smaller size) rather than amplifying a primary
Pick a single focal point / primary metric per region and quiet the rest
Use whitespace/isolation and proximity grouping to separate ranks without removing content
Reduce the number of competing loud signals; not everything can be bold
expected_fix_hints: Demote borders and bold to the few primary cards; make the rest quiet
Group related metrics so the eye reads clusters, not 14 equal items
absent_signals: Do not make the primary metric even louder while leaving the rest loud
Do not delete required metrics to reduce noise

cases.scenario: A pricing page shows three identical filled-blue buttons of equal size: 'Start trial', 'Contact sales', and 'See docs'. Conversion analytics show users hesitate.
cases.context: The business wants 'Start trial' to be the primary action.
cases.question: How should the agent order the actions visually?
expected_flags: Make exactly one primary CTA ('Start trial') visibly dominant in fill/weight/size
Demote the other two to secondary treatment (outline/ghost/text link)
At most one primary CTA per view; secondary actions read as clearly subordinate
Increase the difference along one signal (fill) rather than nudging all three slightly
expected_fix_hints: Keep the filled style only on the primary; outline or text-link the rest
Optionally reduce secondary button size/weight to reinforce rank
absent_signals: Do not leave three equal-weight primary buttons
Do not make all three louder to 'help conversion'

cases.scenario: An article layout uses 11 type sizes between 13px and 19px so 'every level has its own size.' Readers can't tell H2 from H3 from body.
cases.context: Long-form content with multiple heading levels and pull quotes.
cases.question: How should the agent fix the type hierarchy?
expected_flags: Collapse to ~5-7 sizes derived from a single ratio applied to a base size
Choose a ratio loud enough that adjacent levels are perceptibly different (e.g. 1.25-1.333 for long-form)
Too many near-identical sizes dilute hierarchy
Reinforce rank with weight/contrast, not just size, where sizes must stay close
expected_fix_hints: Pick a base (e.g. 16px) and a ratio; generate the steps
Map each step to a semantic level (body, h3, h2, h1, display)
absent_signals: Do not keep 11 hand-picked near-equal sizes
Do not add even more sizes to disambiguate

cases.scenario: A status page conveys all hierarchy through hue alone — the important alert is red, everything else is gray-blue, but all elements are the same size and weight. In grayscale the page reads as flat.
cases.context: Some users have color-vision deficiency; the team only tested in color.
cases.question: How should the agent strengthen the hierarchy?
expected_flags: Hierarchy must survive grayscale — add a non-color signal (size, weight, isolation) to the primary alert
Do not rely on hue alone to carry rank
Verify with a grayscale screenshot that the intended order is retained
Color can reinforce but should not be the sole ordering signal
expected_fix_hints: Increase the alert's size/weight and isolate it with whitespace
Keep color as a reinforcing cue, not the only one
absent_signals: Do not leave hierarchy carried by hue alone
Do not assume color-only ordering is accessible

cases.scenario: A developer argues the landing page hierarchy is correct because the H1 is first in the DOM, but a full-bleed high-contrast promo banner sits visually above and around it, grabbing all attention.
cases.context: Users in tests look at the banner first and miss the headline.
cases.question: How should the agent respond?
expected_flags: Reading order is a property of the rendered surface, not the markup
The eye follows visual cues (contrast, size, position, isolation) regardless of source order
The high-contrast banner outranks the H1 perceptually despite DOM order
Verify by what is noticed first (squint test), then quiet the banner or amplify the H1
expected_fix_hints: Reduce the banner's contrast/size or increase the H1's prominence
Re-run the squint test until the intended element is noticed first
absent_signals: Do not accept DOM order as proof of correct reading order
Do not leave a louder competing element above the intended focal point

cases.scenario: A PM asks the visual-hierarchy owner to choose the brand's heading typeface, define the modular type-scale ratio for the design system, and write the hero headline copy.
cases.context: The team conflates 'hierarchy' with all type and content decisions.
cases.question: How should the agent scope the request?
expected_flags: Typeface selection and defining the type-scale ratio are typography-system's job, not visual-hierarchy's
Writing the headline copy is copywriting/content, out of scope
Offer the in-scope part: how the existing levels should rank on the surface (what the eye sees first)
Correctly redirects rather than answering out of lane
expected_fix_hints: Hand typeface + scale-ratio definition to typography-system
Hand headline copy to a copywriting/content skill
absent_signals: Do not select the typeface or define the scale ratio here
Do not write the headline copy

cases.scenario: A settings form spaces every field and its label with identical gaps, so labels appear to belong equally to the field above and below. Users mis-associate labels with the wrong inputs.
cases.context: The form has many fields grouped into logical sections.
cases.question: How should the agent use spacing to fix grouping?
expected_flags: Apply Gestalt proximity: tighten the label-to-its-field gap and widen the gap between fields/sections
Items closer together read as grouped; equal gaps destroy grouping
Use whitespace/rhythm to signal section boundaries without explicit dividers
Snap spacing to a consistent baseline rhythm for predictable resting points
expected_fix_hints: Reduce intra-group spacing and increase inter-group spacing
Define spacing tokens that encode the grouping relationships
absent_signals: Do not keep uniform spacing that breaks grouping
Do not add dividers everywhere instead of using proximity
